In summary, our research is concerned with
a probability model for peak solar proton event fluxes that can be used to predict the probability that a space mission will be affected by a solar proton event of a specified size.
the statistical description of the distribution of solar proton event peak intensities.

the development of a predictive model for the worst case peak flux of solar proton events that can be used to design a space system that will be radiation-hard against failures caused by solar proton events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the probability that a solar proton event peak will exceed 10/spl times/5.5/spl times/102/sup -2//cm/sup -2/sup /s/sup -1/sup /sr/sup -1 is 0.01, and the corresponding probability for a peak flux greater than 1.0/spl times/103/sup -2 //cm/sup -3 /s/sup 3/sup /sr is 0.1
solar proton peak fluxes are described by a truncated power law with an upper limit that is twice the largest observed peak.

a space system that can tolerate a 10 MeV peak flux of 10/sup -2.5/ cm/super -2/ sr/super -1/ s/super -1/, which is about 2% of the maximum value, will not be affected by any solar proton event that has occurred in the past, and is unlikely to be affected by a future event.
